title: Why a good test can still surprise you
topic: Bayes theorem with a low base rate

scenes.title: Start with the base rate
scenes.narration: Imagine one thousand people. The condition affects one percent of them, so we expect ten people with it and nine hundred ninety without it. These are illustrative assumptions, not clinical data.

scenes.title: A test has two ways to say yes
scenes.narration: Suppose the test detects ninety percent of cases. That gives nine true positives. Its specificity is ninety five percent, so five percent of the other group also test positive.

scenes.title: False positives can outnumber real cases
scenes.narration: Five percent of nine hundred ninety is forty nine point five. Expected counts need not be whole numbers. Compare nine true positives with forty nine point five false positives.

visual.caption: Expected positive results, not observed people.

scenes.title: Update the probability
scenes.narration: Among all positive results, the fraction with the condition is nine divided by fifty eight point five. That is about fifteen point four percent. Bayes theorem combines the base rate with the test evidence.

visual.caption: Changing the base rate changes the answer.
